claim: Spinal stimulation is a promising method to restore motor function after impairment of descending pathways.
source: Spinal stimulation is a promising method to restore motor function after impairment of descending pathways.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Spinal stimulation improves voluntary control of the impaired limb after spinal cord injury in humans.
source: Recent studies have shown that spinal stimulation improves voluntary control of the impaired limb after spinal cord injury in humans (Angeli et al., 2018; Gill et al., 2018; Harkema et al., 2011; Wagner et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Spinal stimulation improves voluntary control of the impaired limb after spinal cord injury in animals.
source: Recent studies have shown that spinal stimulation improves voluntary control of the impaired limb after spinal cord injury in humans (Angeli et al., 2018; Gill et al., 2018; Harkema et al., 2011; Wagner et al., 2018) and animals (Barra et al., 2022; Capogrosso et al., 2016; Courtine et al., 2009; Kasten et al., 2013; McPherson et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2013; van den Brand et al., 2012; Wenger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Motor outputs of spinal stimulation showed excitatory effects in anesthetized animals.
source: Motor outputs of spinal stimulation have been examined extensively and showed excitatory effects in anesthetized animals (epidural spinal cord stimulation: Greiner et al., 2021; intraspinal microstimulation: Moritz et al., 2007; Mushahwar et al., 2004; Zimmermann et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Motor outputs of spinal stimulation showed excitatory effects in spinalized animals.
source: Motor outputs of spinal stimulation have been examined extensively and showed excitatory effects in anesthetized animals (epidural spinal cord stimulation: Greiner et al., 2021; intraspinal microstimulation: Moritz et al., 2007; Mushahwar et al., 2004; Zimmermann et al., 2011), spinalized animals (epidural spinal cord stimulation: Courtine et al., 2009; van den Brand et al., 2012; Capogrosso et al., 2016; Wenger et al., 2016; Barra et al., 2022; intraspinal microstimulation: Nishimura et al., 2013; Kasten et al., 2013; Mushahwar et al., 2004; Loeb et al., 1993; Tresch and Bizzi, 1999; Bizzi et al., 1991; Giszter et al., 1993; Mussa-Ivaldi et al., 1994)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Motor outputs of spinal stimulation showed excitatory effects in humans.
source: Motor outputs of spinal stimulation have been examined extensively and showed excitatory effects in anesthetized animals (epidural spinal cord stimulation: Greiner et al., 2021; intraspinal microstimulation: Moritz et al., 2007; Mushahwar et al., 2004; Zimmermann et al., 2011), spinalized animals (epidural spinal cord stimulation: Courtine et al., 2009; van den Brand et al., 2012; Capogrosso et al., 2016; Wenger et al., 2016; Barra et al., 2022; intraspinal microstimulation: Nishimura et al., 2013; Kasten et al., 2013; Mushahwar et al., 2004; Loeb et al., 1993; Tresch and Bizzi, 1999; Bizzi et al., 1991; Giszter et al., 1993; Mussa-Ivaldi et al., 1994), and humans (epidural spinal cord stimulation: Angeli et al., 2018; Gill et al., 2018; Harkema et al., 2011; Wagner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Under conditions of anesthesia, spinalization, or in humans with complete spinal cord injury, the excitability of motoneurons is too low to observe the effect of inhibitory spinal interneurons on motor outputs.
source: Under these conditions, however, the excitability of motoneurons is too low to observe the effect of inhibitory spinal interneurons on motor outputs, thus, investigations during voluntary movements are necessary.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of prior studies.

claim: Paresis is a weakness of voluntary movements caused by partial lesion of descending pathways.
source: Paresis is a weakness of voluntary movements caused by partial lesion of descending pathways
evidence: This is a definition based on established medical knowledge.

claim: Paresis is a major symptom in spinal cord injury.
source: Paresis is a weakness of voluntary movements caused by partial lesion of descending pathways and is a major symptom in spinal cord injury (National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center, 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to statistical data.

claim: Paresis is a major symptom in stroke.
source: Paresis is a weakness of voluntary movements caused by partial lesion of descending pathways and is a major symptom in spinal cord injury (National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center, 2021) and stroke (Ramnemark et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Paresis is a major target for therapeutic spinal stimulation.
source: Paresis is a weakness of voluntary movements caused by partial lesion of descending pathways and is a major symptom in spinal cord injury (National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center, 2021) and stroke (Ramnemark et al., 1998), as well as a major target for therapeutic spinal stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical relevance of paresis.

claim: Individuals with paresis have difficulty controlling their limb movements.
source: Although individuals with paresis have difficulty controlling their limb movements, they can produce weak muscle activity driven by the preserved descending pathways.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge about paresis.

claim: Individuals with paresis can produce weak muscle activity driven by preserved descending pathways.
source: Although individuals with paresis have difficulty controlling their limb movements, they can produce weak muscle activity driven by the preserved descending pathways.
evidence: This is based on established clinical knowledge about paresis.

claim: The modulation of muscle responses to spinal stimulation by descending commands has not been fully clarified.
source: Although a few studies have examined spinal stimulation in awake animals (Kato et al., 2020; Sharma and Shah, 2021; Barra et al., 2022), the modulation of muscle responses to spinal stimulation by descending commands has not been fully clarified.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: Descending commands for controlling voluntary limb movements are generated in the motor cortex.
source: Descending commands for controlling voluntary limb movements are generated in the motor cortex and activate spinal motoneurons and interneurons.
evidence: This is based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Descending commands activate spinal motoneurons and interneurons.
source: Descending commands for controlling voluntary limb movements are generated in the motor cortex and activate spinal motoneurons and interneurons.
evidence: This is based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Neural activity in the primary motor cortex represents the direction of joint movement.
source: Numerous studies have shown that neural activity in the primary motor cortex represents various movement parameters such as the direction of joint movement (Caminiti et al., 1990; Cisek et al., 2003; Crammond and Kalaska, 1996; Fu et al., 1993; Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Schwartz et al., 1988)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Neural activity in the primary motor cortex represents the amount of muscle activity.
source: Numerous studies have shown that neural activity in the primary motor cortex represents various movement parameters such as the direction of joint movement (Caminiti et al., 1990; Cisek et al., 2003; Crammond and Kalaska, 1996; Fu et al., 1993; Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Georgopoulos et al., 1986; Schwartz et al., 1988) and the amount of muscle activity (Buys et al., 1986; Cheney et al., 1985b; Fetz and Cheney, 1980; Lemon et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Movement parameters during voluntary movement modify the motor outputs evoked by spinal stimulation.
source: We hypothesized that such parameters during voluntary movement modify the motor outputs evoked by spinal stimulation.
evidence: This is the hypothesis of the study.

claim: A platinum electrode array was chronically implanted in the subdural space over the right-side dorsal rootlets of the cervical enlargement.
source: A platinum electrode array was chronically implanted in the subdural space over the right-side dorsal rootlets of the cervical enlargement (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is shown in Figure 1A, B.

claim: Muscle responses of the right upper limb and wrist torques induced by spinal stimulation were investigated under anesthesia.
source: We investigated muscle responses of the right upper limb and wrist torques induced by spinal stimulation to the cervical enlargement under anesthesia and during an isometric, 2D, eight-target, wrist torque tracking task (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Muscle responses of the right upper limb and wrist torques induced by spinal stimulation were investigated during an isometric, 2D, eight-target, wrist torque tracking task.
source: We investigated muscle responses of the right upper limb and wrist torques induced by spinal stimulation to the cervical enlargement under anesthesia and during an isometric, 2D, eight-target, wrist torque tracking task (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Subdural spinal stimuli induced limb movements under anesthesia.
source: Subdural spinal stimuli consisting of three constant-current, biphasic square-wave pulses of 333 Hz with 0.2 ms duration were delivered to the anesthetized monkeys through a single electrode on the spinal cord.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and results.

claim: Electrodes located rostrally tended to induce movements in the proximal arm joints.
source: The electrodes located rostrally tended to induce movements in the proximal arm joints, while caudal electrodes induced movements in distal finger joints.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Table 1.

claim: Caudal electrodes induced movements in distal finger joints.
source: The electrodes located rostrally tended to induce movements in the proximal arm joints, while caudal electrodes induced movements in distal finger joints.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Table 1.

claim: The evoked movements showed somatotopic representations.
source: Overall, the evoked movements showed somatotopic representations as described previously (Kato et al., 2020; Sunshine et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: Spinal stimulation produced facilitation and/or suppression effects on muscle activities in multiple muscles.
source: Spinal stimulation (150–1350 µA) produced facilitation and/or suppression effects on muscle activities in multiple muscles.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of muscle responses showed directional tuning.
source: The magnitude of these muscle responses showed directional tuning and positively correlated with the level of background muscle activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of muscle responses positively correlated with the level of background muscle activity.
source: The magnitude of these muscle responses showed directional tuning and positively correlated with the level of background muscle activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Spinal stimulation boosted torque production in the direction corresponding with the direction of voluntary torque production.
source: Moreover, spinal stimulation boosted torque production in the direction corresponding with the direction of voluntary torque production.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Spinal stimulation at an appropriate current is beneficial in a partial lesion of descending pathways to compensate for reduced descending commands.
source: These findings suggest that spinal stimulation at an appropriate current is beneficial in a partial lesion of descending pathways to compensate for reduced descending commands by activating excitatory and inhibitory trans-synaptic connections to spinal motoneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Of the 1008 muscular conditions recorded, 515 showed only Facilitation.
source: Of the 1008 muscular conditions recorded over all the experiments, 515 muscular conditions in all 16 muscles showed only Facilitation (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 23 muscular conditions in 13 muscles showed only Suppression in all peripheral targets.
source: 23 muscular conditions in 13 muscles showed only Suppression in all peripheral targets (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 469 muscular conditions in 16 muscles changed the type of PStEs depending on the direction.
source: A total of 469 muscular conditions in 16 muscles changed the type of PStEs, Facilitation or Suppression, depending on the direction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only one muscular condition in the intrinsic hand muscles showed no response in any of the target locations.
source: Only one muscular condition in the intrinsic hand muscles showed no response in any of the target locations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Significant PDs were observed in 603 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for Facilitation.
source: Significant PDs were observed in the 603 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for Facilitation (Spinal PD of Facilitation)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Significant PDs were observed in 333 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for Suppression.
source: Significant PDs were observed in the 603 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for Facilitation (Spinal PD of Facilitation), 333 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for Suppression (Spinal PD of Suppression)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Significant PDs were observed in 1006 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for background EMG.
source: Significant PDs were observed in the 603 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for Facilitation (Spinal PD of Facilitation), 333 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for Suppression (Spinal PD of Suppression), and 1006 muscular conditions in 16 muscles for background EMG.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The distributions of Spinal PDs of Facilitation were significantly nonuniform and tuned in the ulnar direction.
source: The distributions of Spinal PDs of Facilitation (top-left in Figure 2D) and Suppression (top-right in Figure 2D) were significantly nonuniform and tuned in the ulnar and radial directions, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The distributions of Spinal PDs of Suppression were significantly nonuniform and tuned in the radial direction.
source: The distributions of Spinal PDs of Facilitation (top-left in Figure 2D) and Suppression (top-right in Figure 2D) were significantly nonuniform and tuned in the ulnar and radial directions, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Normalized Spinal PDs were significantly tuned around 0°.
source: Indeed, Normalized Spinal PDs were significantly tuned around the predicted value of 0° (bottom panels in Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Muscle responses induced by spinal stimulation were tuned depending on the directions of voluntary torque production.
source: Therefore, we conclude that muscle responses induced by spinal stimulation were tuned depending on the directions of voluntary torque production and that the PDs of induced muscle responses were identical to the PDs of voluntary activation of the corresponding muscle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The PDs of induced muscle responses were identical to the PDs of voluntary activation of the corresponding muscle.
source: Therefore, we conclude that muscle responses induced by spinal stimulation were tuned depending on the directions of voluntary torque production and that the PDs of induced muscle responses were identical to the PDs of voluntary activation of the corresponding muscle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Directional tuning of PStEs was modulated depending on the current intensity.
source: Directional tuning of PStEs was modulated depending on the current intensity.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Suppression was dominant at lower currents.
source: Suppression was dominant at lower currents, while Facilitation was dominant at higher currents (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Facilitation was dominant at higher currents.
source: Suppression was dominant at lower currents, while Facilitation was dominant at higher currents (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The magnitudes of Facilitation increased with increasing current intensities.
source: The magnitudes of Facilitation increased, and the magnitudes of Suppression decreased with increasing current intensities.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The magnitudes of Suppression decreased with increasing current intensities.
source: The magnitudes of Facilitation increased, and the magnitudes of Suppression decreased with increasing current intensities.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Spinal PDs of Suppression and Facilitation at lower currents corresponded to the PDs of background EMG.
source: In addition, Spinal PDs of Suppression (70 and 180 μA in Figure 3A; 70 μA in Figure 3B) and Facilitation (1000 μA in Figure 3A; 200 and 1000 μA in Figure 3B) at lower currents corresponded to the PDs of background EMG
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Stimulation at higher currents indicated either no PD or a significant PD at almost the opposite direction of the PD for background EMG.
source: while stimulation at higher currents indicated either no PD (1700 μA in Figure 3A) or a significant PD at almost the opposite direction of the PD for background EMG (1700 μA in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The percentage of 'Facilitation' increased as the stimulus current increased.
source: The percentage of 'Facilitation' increased and the percentage of other types decreased as the stimulus current increased (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The magnitudes of Facilitation increased as the current intensity increased.
source: The magnitudes of Facilitation (left panel in Figure 3D) increased as the current intensity increased.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The magnitudes of Suppression at higher currents tended to decrease compared to those at lower current.
source: The magnitudes of Suppression at higher currents tended to decrease compared to those at lower current (right panel in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Spinal PDs for Facilitation and Suppression at lower current (<1350 μA) exhibited significant nonuniform distributions toward ulnar and radial directions, respectively.
source: The Spinal PDs for Facilitation and Suppression at lower current (<1350 μA) exhibited significant nonuniform distributions toward ulnar and radial directions, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Normalized Spinal PDs showed commonly nonuniform distributions around 0° at lower currents (<1350 μA).
source: The Normalized Spinal PDs showed commonly nonuniform distributions around 0° (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Spinal PD for Facilitation at higher currents (≥1350 μA) showed uniform distributions.
source: In contrast, Spinal PD for Facilitation at higher currents (≥1350 μA) showed uniform distributions (bottom-left panel in Figure 3E)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Normalized Spinal PD for Facilitation at higher currents (≥1350 μA) exhibited the opposite to PD of background EMG.
source: and the Normalized Spinal PD for Facilitation exhibited the opposite to PD of background EMG (bottom-left panel in Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Relations between the Spinal PD and the PD of background EMG changed by current intensity.
source: Thus, relations between the Spinal PD and the PD of background EMG changed by current intensity, implying that recruited neural elements depend on current intensity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Recruited neural elements depend on current intensity.
source: Thus, relations between the Spinal PD and the PD of background EMG changed by current intensity, implying that recruited neural elements depend on current intensity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Stimulation at rostral sites exhibited larger magnitudes of Facilitation effects into the rostrally innervated muscles than stimulation at caudal sites.
source: Stimulation at rostral sites exhibited larger magnitudes of Facilitation effects into the rostrally innervated muscles than stimulation at caudal sites (Figure 4E, left panel).
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In the caudally innervated muscles, stimulation at caudal sites produced larger magnitudes of PStEs on both Facilitation and Suppression than stimulation at rostral sites.
source: Similarly, in the caudally innervated muscles, stimulation at caudal sites produced larger magnitudes of PStEs on both Facilitation and Suppression than stimulation at rostral sites (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Regardless of stimulus sites, almost all Spinal PDs tuned to directions corresponding to the PDs of background EMG.
source: Regardless of stimulus sites, almost all Spinal PDs tuned to directions corresponding to the PDs of background EMG (first and fourth row panels in Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: The Normalized Spinal PDs showed nonuniform distributions around 0° regardless of stimulus sites.
source: That is, the Normalized Spinal PDs showed nonuniform distributions around 0° (third and sixth row panels in Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: On stimulation at caudal sites, Spinal PD of Facilitation in rostrally innervated muscles was opposite to the PD of background EMG.
source: On stimulation at caudal sites, Spinal PD of Facilitation in rostrally innervated muscles was opposite to the PD of background EMG (compare between top-left panel and middle-left panel in caudal site of Figure 4G)
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The Normalized Spinal PDs for Facilitation in rostrally innervated muscles on stimulation at caudal sites exhibited nonuniform distributions around 180°.
source: and the Normalized Spinal PDs for Facilitation exhibited nonuniform distributions around 180° (Figure 4G, bottom-left panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Stimulation at caudal sites produced Spinal PDs for Suppression tuned with radial directions into the rostrally innervated muscles.
source: On the other hand, stimulation at caudal sites produced Spinal PDs for Suppression tuned with radial directions into the rostrally innervated muscles (top-right panel in caudal site of Figure 4G), which was similar to the PD for background EMG (middle-right panel in caudal site of Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The magnitude of PStEs increased as background EMG increased.
source: Regardless of the type of PStEs, the magnitude of PStEs increased as background EMG increased (right panels in Figure 5A–C, two-sided Pearson's correlation, Figure 5A, r=0.950, p=0.01; Figure 5B, r=0.997, p=2.00 × 10–4; Figure 5C, r=0.999, p=4.63 × 10–5)
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Most muscular conditions showed significant positive correlations between the magnitudes of PStEs and background EMGs.
source: and most muscular conditions showed significant positive correlations between the magnitudes of PStEs and background EMGs (hatched bars in Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The magnitudes of the induced muscle responses altered by the direction of voluntary torques are tuned by the excitability of spinal motoneurons.
source: These results indicate that the magnitudes of the induced muscle responses altered by the direction of voluntary torques are tuned by the excitability of spinal motoneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Lower current (70 μA) produced Suppression and showed a strong positive correlation between the magnitudes of PStEs and background EMGs.
source: Lower current (70 μA) produced Suppression and showed a strong positive correlation between the magnitudes of PStEs and background EMGs (Figure 6A, two-sided Pearson's correlation, r=0.995, p=4.00 × 10–4).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Medium and higher current stimulations induced Facilitation and resulted in a saturation of Facilitation, with no significant correlations.
source: On the other hand, medium (150 μA and 1000 μA) and higher (1700 μA) current stimulations induced Facilitation and resulted in a saturation of Facilitation, with no significant correlations (two-sided Pearson's correlation, Figure 6B, r=0.862, p=0.06; Figure 6C, r=0.611, p=0.27; Figure 6D, r=–0.788, p=0.11).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Higher currents at 1700 μA tended to reduce the magnitudes of Facilitation on higher background EMG.
source: Moreover, higher currents at 1700 μA (Figure 6D) tended to reduce the magnitudes of Facilitation on higher background EMG.
evidence: This is based on observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Most muscular conditions at lower currents (<1350 μA) showed a significant positive relationship in all PStEs types.
source: Most muscular conditions at lower currents (<1350 μA) showed a significant positive relationship in all PStEs types (first to third row panels in Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The distribution of correlation coefficient at higher currents (≥1350 μA) showed a uniform distribution that included a negative relationship between the magnitudes of PStEs and background EMGs.
source: In contrast, the distribution of correlation coefficient at higher currents (≥1350 μA) showed a uniform distribution that included a negative relationship between the magnitudes of PStEs and background EMGs (bottom-left panel in Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Stimulus-induced muscle responses at lower currents were amplified depending on the amount of descending commands to spinal motoneurons.
source: Consequently, these results indicate that stimulus-induced muscle responses at lower currents were amplified depending on the amount of descending commands to spinal motoneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Stimulus-induced muscle responses at higher current were attenuated on higher background EMG.
source: On the other hand, stimulus-induced muscle responses at higher current were attenuated on higher background EMG.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Spinal stimulation induced significant Evoked Torque.
source: The length and direction of arrows represent magnitudes and directions of Evoked Torque (a value near each arrow in the inner peripheral panels in Figure 7B–D indicates the direction of Evoked Torque), respectively, and, together, indicate that spinal stimulation induced significant Evoked Torque.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Spinal stimulation at 110 μA tended to induce Suppression effects on muscles with higher background EMG.
source: Spinal stimulation at 110 μA tended to induce Suppression effects on muscles with higher background EMG (outer peripheral panels in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The directions of Evoked Torque at 110 μA were opposite to the directions of voluntary torque and were converged to the center target.
source: The directions of Evoked Torque were opposite to the directions of voluntary torque and were converged to the center target where the wrist is relaxed (inner peripheral panels in Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Spinal stimulation at 300 μA mainly induced Facilitation effects on muscles with higher background EMG.
source: In another case, spinal stimulation at 300 μA mainly induced Facilitation effects on muscles with higher background EMG (outer peripheral panels in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The directions of the Evoked Torque at 300 μA were similar to the directions of voluntary torque.
source: and the directions of the Evoked Torque were similar to the directions of voluntary torque independent of the direction of the Evoked Torque at the center target (center and inner peripheral panels in Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Stimulation at 1700 μA exhibited large magnitudes of Facilitation in all muscles for all targets.
source: Stimulation at 1700 μA exhibited large magnitudes of Facilitation in all muscles for all targets (outer peripheral panels in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Evoked Torques at 1700 μA displayed ulnar-flexion directions regardless of the presence/absence or the direction of voluntary torque.
source: and the Evoked Torques displayed ulnar-flexion directions regardless of the presence/absence or the direction of voluntary torque (center and inner peripheral panels in Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The magnitudes of Evoked Torque for the peripheral targets increased as the current intensity increased.
source: Population data showed that the magnitudes of Evoked Torque for the peripheral targets increased as the current intensity increased (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Lower currents (<150 μA) exhibited uniform distribution in the directions of the Evoked Torque.
source: Lower currents (<150 μA) exhibited uniform distribution in the directions of the Evoked Torque (top-left panel in Figure 7F)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Lower currents (<150 μA) were opposite to the directions of voluntary torque.
source: and were opposite to the directions of voluntary torque (top-right panel in Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Medium currents (150–1350 μA) induced Evoked Torque predominately toward the ulnar-flexor direction.
source: Medium currents (150–1350 μA) induced Evoked Torque predominately toward the ulnar-flexor direction (second and third-left panels in Figure 7F)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The directions of Normalized Torque at medium currents (150–1350 μA) corresponded to the direction of voluntary torque.
source: and the directions of Normalized Torque corresponded to the direction of voluntary torque (second- and third-right panels in Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: High currents (≥1350 μA) displayed Evoked Torques only toward the ulnar-flexion direction regardless of the direction of voluntary torque.
source: Since high currents (≥1350 μA) displayed Evoked Torques only toward the ulnar-flexion direction regardless of the direction of voluntary torque (bottom-left panel in Figure 7F)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The direction of Normalized Torques at high currents (≥1350 μA) showed uniform distributions.
source: the direction of Normalized Torques showed uniform distributions (bottom-right panel in Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: At medium current (150–1350 μA), spinal stimulation boosted torque outputs in the same direction as on-going voluntary torque production.
source: Accordingly, magnitudes and directions of stimulus-induced wrist torques were modulated according to the direction of voluntary torque and current intensity. At medium current (150–1350 μA), spinal stimulation boosted torque outputs in the same direction as on-going voluntary torque production.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The onset latency of the PStEs was found to shorten as the current increased.
source: Regardless of whether the current intensity changed the type of PStEs (Figure 8A and B), the onset latency of the PStEs was found to shorten as the current increased.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Stimulation at lower current (70 μA) clearly changed onset latencies of PStEs depending on directions of voluntary torque.
source: In this example, stimulation at lower current (70 μA) clearly changed onset latencies of PStEs depending on directions of voluntary torque, while onset latencies of PStEs at higher currents (1000 and 1700 μA) were similar among different directions.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Onset latencies of PStEs at higher currents (1000 and 1700 μA) were similar among different directions.
source: In this example, stimulation at lower current (70 μA) clearly changed onset latencies of PStEs depending on directions of voluntary torque, while onset latencies of PStEs at higher currents (1000 and 1700 μA) were similar among different directions.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The median onset latency of Facilitation effects was shorter than that of Suppression effects at all current intensities.
source: The median onset latency of Facilitation effects was shorter than that of Suppression effects at all current intensities.
evidence: This is based on population analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The median onset latencies of Facilitation effects became shorter as stimulus currents increased.
